name: RethinkDB
vendor: RethinkDB community (copyright held by the Linux Foundation)

foundation.via: Bought from the defunct RethinkDB company by the CNCF and contributed to the Linux Foundation

status.note: Volunteer-maintained: the last feature release, 2.4, was in December 2019, and 2.4.5 (November 2025) only fixed builds on newer platforms.

summary: A clustered JSON document database whose queries can stay open as changefeeds, pushing every change to the client instead of the app polling for it.
intro: RethinkDB stores JSON documents in tables and is queried with ReQL, a query language built from method chains in the host language: `r.table('game').orderBy({index: 'score'}).limit(3)` in JavaScript, the same chain in Python, Ruby or Java. Add `.changes()` to most queries and the server keeps them open as a changefeed, sending the old and new value of every document that enters, leaves or changes the result. That is the feature it was built around: a leaderboard, chat room or dashboard subscribes to a query and gets updates pushed over the driver connection.

A table is range-sharded on its primary key across servers, and each shard has one primary replica and any number of secondaries, configured with `reconfigure(shards=…, replicas=…)` or from the built-in web console. Cluster configuration is kept with Raft, and when enough voting replicas remain a failed primary is replaced automatically. Writes are atomic per document only; by default they are acknowledged once a majority of replicas have them on disk, while reads come from the primary’s memory unless you ask for `read_mode: 'majority'`, which makes single-document operations linearizable. Data lives in B-trees on a log-structured storage engine with its own cache, so tables can be much larger than RAM.

The company behind it shut down in October 2016. The CNCF bought the code and copyrights in February 2017, relicensed them from AGPLv3 to Apache 2.0 and gave the project to the Linux Foundation, where volunteers have kept it alive since. They shipped 2.4 in December 2019 with write hooks, then only fix and build releases; 2.4.5 in November 2025 changed nothing but packaging. Commits still land in 2026, mostly tests and CI, so it is maintained but not moving forward.
strengths: Changefeeds on ordinary queries, including filtered and ordered ones, so realtime updates need no separate pub/sub system
ReQL composes in your own language, with joins, aggregation and map/reduce running in parallel across shards
Sharding, replication and automatic failover are built in and can be changed live from the web console or the API
Apache 2.0 with copyright held by the Linux Foundation, so no single company can relicense it
limits: Little development: no feature release since 2.4 in 2019, a small volunteer team, and official drivers for only JavaScript, Python, Ruby and Java
No multi-document transactions; a single query is not atomic across the documents it touches
The default `read_mode` of `single` can return writes a failover later loses; strong reads need `majority` and cost latency
Changefeeds are not a durable log: a client that disconnects misses changes and has to re-read, unlike a Kafka topic or a CDC stream

specs.data-model: JSON documents in tables, each with a primary key
specs.query-language: ReQL, chained methods in the client language, with `.changes()` for live queries
specs.wire-protocol: Its own JSON protocol over TCP, used by the drivers
specs.secondary-indexes: Secondary, compound, multi and geospatial indexes
specs.transactions: Atomic per document; none across documents
specs.consistency: Majority write acks by default; reads from the primary’s memory unless `read_mode: majority`
specs.scaling: Range sharding on the primary key across servers
specs.replication: One primary and many secondaries per shard; automatic failover, configuration kept with Raft
specs.storage-engine: Log-structured storage with B-trees and its own cache
specs.deployment: Self-hosted; no managed service since the company closed

story: Slava Akhmechet and Michael Glukhovsky started RethinkDB in 2009 with seed money from Y Combinator. It began as a storage engine for MySQL tuned for solid-state drives, then became a distributed JSON database; the first public release, 1.2, came in November 2012. Changefeeds became its defining feature, and the repository still calls it “the open-source database for the realtime web”. Version 2.0, in April 2015, was the first release the company called production-ready.

The company never found a business. On 5 October 2016 Akhmechet announced that RethinkDB the company was shutting down and that much of the engineering team was joining Stripe, while the code stayed open source. In February 2017 the CNCF paid $25,000 for the source code, copyrights and assets, relicensed them from AGPLv3, which some companies had refused to use, to Apache 2.0, and contributed the project to the Linux Foundation. Community maintainers released 2.3.6, the first release under community governance, then 2.4 in December 2019 with write hooks, and since then fix releases up to 2.4.5 in November 2025.

choices.choice: Push query results, don’t make apps poll
choices.why: Realtime apps built on other databases had to poll or bolt on a message broker; changefeeds let the query itself be the subscription.

choices.choice: A query language embedded in the host language
choices.why: ReQL is built from ordinary method calls, so queries compose like code and can’t be broken by string concatenation.

choices.choice: Relicense to Apache 2.0 after the shutdown
choices.why: AGPLv3 had kept some companies from using or contributing; the CNCF called the purchase a chance “to salvage an enormous investment with a small incremental contribution”.

timeline.text: Founded with Y Combinator seed funding, first as a MySQL storage engine for SSDs
The company shuts down; engineers join Stripe (October)
CNCF buys the code for $25,000, relicenses it to Apache 2.0 and contributes it to the Linux Foundation (February)
RethinkDB 2.4 with write hooks (December), the last feature release
